summary: Discusses an implementation approach to Telnet option negotiation, a way to avoid loops and confusion when both sides ask for options. It proposes no protocol change and is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people keep asking each other to change settings and can get stuck repeating. This is a trick to make them agree without going in circles.

questions: how to prevent telnet infinite loops
what is wantyes state in telnet
subtitle: A practical approach to prevent infinite loops in TELNET option negotiation.

tldr.problem: TELNET's option negotiation mechanism allows either side to request options be enabled or disabled, which can create infinite loops where both sides keep disagreeing and sending requests back and forth forever.
tldr.mechanism: The Q Method tracks negotiation state separately from enabled/disabled state, forbids initiating new requests while one is pending, and buffers user requests in a simple queue so the implementation waits for responses before sending contradictory requests.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides concrete rules and a worked example state machine, allowing implementors to write TELNET that avoids negotiation loops while preserving full functionality. It influenced TELNET implementations but was never formally standardized.

today: RFC 1143 remains Experimental. While it influenced TELNET implementations and provided valuable guidance on option negotiation, it was never formally adopted as a standard. Most modern TELNET implementations use similar state-machine approaches inspired by or equivalent to the Q Method.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 1143 discusses an implementation approach to option negotiation in the TELNET protocol (RFC 854). Unlike RFC 854, which only provides guidelines, this RFC identifies problems with option negotiation loops and presents a concrete method to prevent them. The RFC does not change the TELNET protocol itself; it only shows how to implement existing TELNET correctly.

This RFC is aimed at TELNET implementors. The most valuable contributions are: first, concrete examples of how option negotiation loops occur, and second, a complete working state machine (called the Q Method) that prevents loops. An implementor who follows the state machine in this RFC can safely avoid compliance worries and focus on correct behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: TELNET lets both computers ask each other to turn options on or off. Sometimes this creates an endless argument. This memo explains the problem and shows a simple way to avoid it.

sections.title: The Negotiation Loop Problem
sections.content:
TELNET options are negotiated separately for each side of the connection. The side sending WILL and WONT commands controls its own side; the side sending DO and DONT controls the other side. The RFC describes two concrete loop examples that occur in practice.

Loop Example 1: Both sides start with an option enabled. One side sends DONT to disable it on the other side, and the other side responds with WONT. Then the first side requests DO (enable it again), the other side rejects with WONT, and the pattern repeats: DONT DO DO forever in one direction and WONT WONT WILL WONT forever in the other. Both sides have followed RFC 854 but end up looping.

Loop Example 2: A user rapidly requests enable, disable, enable for an option. The TELNET implementation sends WILL WONT WILL, the other side agrees with DO DONT DO, but by the time the responses arrive, both sides have forgotten about the negotiation. They see disagreements and send DO DONT while both think negotiation is complete, looping forever.

RFC 1143 identifies the root causes: implementations that disable immediately and forget the negotiation, and implementations that allow new requests while one is still pending.
sections.plainLanguage: When one computer sends WILL and the other sends DONT, one of them might decide to try again. Or when a user changes their mind quickly, the computers can get out of sync and end up disagreeing forever.

sections.title: Core Compliance Rules
sections.content:
RFC 1143 establishes several MUST rules derived from RFC 854 and extended to prevent loops. First: Obey refusals. If the other side sends DONT or WONT in response to a WILL or DO, the option must not be enabled. Second: Remember negotiation state separately from enabled state. The state of negotiating for enable is different from having the option enabled; during negotiation, the option's effects must not be used.

Third: Do not initiate a new request about an option that is already under negotiation. An implementation must wait for a response before sending a new WILL/WONT/DO/DONT command about that option. Fourth: Remember starting a DONT/WONT negotiation. Unlike DO/WILL, it is not obvious that one must remember DONT/WONT, but neglecting it allows Loop Example 1 to occur.

Fifth: Do not automatically respond to rejection by submitting a new request. New requests should come from user input or process decisions, not automatically after a rejection.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask for something and get refused, really refuse it. Keep two kinds of memory: whether you are asking, and whether you have it. Do not ask again while you are still waiting for an answer. Remember that you asked to disable something, not just whether it is disabled.

sections.title: The Q Method: Queue System
sections.content:
To prevent Loop Example 2 while preserving user responsiveness, RFC 1143 proposes the Q Method, which adds a simple request queue. While an option is under negotiation, if the user or process makes a new request to change it, the implementation does not send a new command to the network. Instead, it remembers the request internally in a queue.

The queue is minimal: it need only remember whether the opposite request is queued (a single bit: EMPTY or OPPOSITE). This works because requests must alternate: there is no point in enabling an option, disabling it, and enabling it again when just enabling it is simpler. If the user makes multiple requests in quick succession, each new request either adds the opposite to the queue or forgets the previous one. Only a single opposite request needs to be remembered.

When the pending negotiation receives a response, if the queue indicates a different state is desired, the implementation sends that request immediately and empties the queue. Crucially, these queued requests do not violate RFC 854's rule against automatic request regeneration, because they represent delayed effects of actual user or process commands, not automatic loop-breaking.

Implementations SHOULD support the queue, though MAY allow it to be disabled. When disabled, queued requests should still be handled at negotiation completion.
sections.plainLanguage: While the computer is waiting for an answer, remember if the user changed their mind to the opposite. When the answer comes back, if the user wanted the opposite, send that now.

sections.title: State Machine and Implementation Example
sections.content:
RFC 1143 provides a complete reference implementation as a finite-state machine with four states per side: NO (disabled, not negotiating), WANTNO (negotiating to disable), WANTYES (negotiating to enable), and YES (enabled, not negotiating). Each side maintains two variables: state (one of the four) and a queue bit (EMPTY or OPPOSITE if in a negotiating state).

The state machine defines exact responses for each combination of (state, queue, incoming command). For example, receiving WILL while in state NO means the other side wants to enable. The implementation checks if it agrees: if yes, set state to YES and send DO; if no, send DONT. Receiving WONT while in state WANTYES (waiting for yes) with queue EMPTY means the request was refused; set state to NO and do nothing. If queue is OPPOSITE, handle the queued disable request: set state to WANTNO, empty queue, and send DONT.

The RFC provides similar rules for DO/DONT commands (which control the other side's option) and for user requests to enable or disable. An implementor who directly translates this state machine into code is guaranteed compliance with the RFC and absence of negotiation loops.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a simple table: for each of four states, and for each kind of message you receive or user request, here is what you do next. Follow the table and you will not loop.
